title: Dial Distance
statement: A combination lock has a dial with 2^bits settings, each shown as a bits-bit number. The dial is turned one click at a time from click 0 up to click 2^bits - 1, and after the last click it wraps around to click 0. The setting displayed at click k is k XOR (k >> 1), that is, k XOR-ed with k shifted right by one bit. For every pair [a, b] of settings, return the fewest clicks needed to turn the dial from setting a to setting b, turning in whichever direction is shorter.

examples.explanation: Setting 6 shows at click 4 and setting 9 at click 14, so they are 10 clicks apart one way and 22 the other way around the dial, and the answer is 10. Setting 17 shows at click 30 and setting 3 at click 2, so they are 28 clicks apart one way and 4 the other way around the dial, and the answer is 4.
A one-bit dial has clicks 0 and 1 showing settings 0 and 1, one click apart. A setting is zero clicks from itself.

hints.content: Could you find which click shows a given setting without turning the dial from click 0? Look at what the formula does to each individual bit.
Walking the dial click by click costs up to 2^30 steps for a single query. You need the click number of a setting directly.
The formula keeps the top bit and XORs every other bit with the bit above it. Read it backwards from the top: each click bit is the setting bit XOR the click bit just above.
Unrolling that gives click = setting XOR (setting >> 1) XOR (setting >> 2) XOR ... Doubling the shift each time (1, 2, 4, 8, 16) folds all of them in five steps.
With both click numbers, one direction takes |clickA - clickB| clicks and the other takes 2^bits minus that. Return the smaller. Use 2 ** bits for the dial size.

testCases.explanation: Two pairs on a 5-bit dial, each solved by locating both click numbers.
The smallest dial and a setting compared with itself.
Setting 4 shows at click 7, one click before the dial wraps to click 0, so the short way round is 1.
Every setting of a 3-bit dial measured from setting 0, covering forward, wrapped and opposite distances.
Extremes of a 30-bit dial, including the opposite setting and the last click.
The largest query list on a 30-bit dial: walking the dial click by click would take about a billion steps per query.
The largest query list where every pair names the same setting twice, so every answer is 0.
A mid-size dial where a click-by-click walk is slow but finishes.
All sixteen pairs on a 2-bit dial.

solutions.title: Turn the dial from click 0
solutions.intuition: Generate the settings in click order until both targets have appeared, remembering their click numbers.
solutions.approach: For each pair, loop click from 0 to 2^bits - 1, compute click XOR (click >> 1), and record the click where it equals a and where it equals b. Take the forward distance modulo 2^bits and return the smaller of it and its complement.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(pairs * 2^bits), about a billion steps per pair at 30 bits
commonMistakes: Forgetting that the dial wraps, so the distance is the smaller of the two directions.
Treating the setting itself as the click number, which is only true for the first two clicks.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Simulating the lock is the safest way to understand the sequence and is exact, but each query walks up to 2^bits clicks. With 30 bits that is more than a billion steps, so the click number must be computed from the setting instead.

steps.title: Walk
steps.content: On a 1-bit dial the clicks 0 and 1 show settings 0 and 1.

steps.title: Measure
steps.content: Setting 0 is at click 0 and setting 1 at click 1, a forward distance of 1 and a backward distance of 1.

solutions.title: Decode the click with a prefix XOR
solutions.intuition: Each click bit is the XOR of all setting bits at or above it, so folding the setting onto itself with shifts recovers the click.
solutions.approach: Compute click = setting ^ (setting >> 1), then ^= click >> 2, >> 4, >> 8, >> 16. Take apart = |clickA - clickB| and return min(apart, 2^bits - apart) for every pair.
solutions.pseudocode:
clickOf(s): c = s; c ^= c >> 1; c ^= c >> 2; c ^= c >> 4; c ^= c >> 8; c ^= c >> 16; return c
for (a, b): apart = abs(clickOf(a) - clickOf(b)); answer = min(apart, 2^bits - apart)
solutions.timeComplexity: O(pairs) with a constant five folding steps per setting
commonMistakes: Stopping after the single XOR with setting >> 1, which only undoes one level of the formula.
Returning the forward distance without considering the wrap-around.
Treating the XOR of the two settings as the distance.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The encoder XORs each bit with its upper neighbour, so the decoder must XOR each bit with everything above it, which is a prefix XOR from the top. Shifting by 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 and XOR-ing builds that prefix in five operations for a 31-bit value. Since the clicks form a cycle, the answer is the shorter of the two arcs between the click numbers.

steps.title: Decode the first setting
steps.content: For bits = 5, setting 6 decodes to click 4 and setting 9 decodes to click 14.

steps.title: Pick the shorter arc
steps.content: The arcs are 10 and 22, so the answer is 10.
